bibliographic.title: Hospitalists Are Already Using AI—Why Implementation Will Determine Its Impact
bibliographic.authors: Anna Maw; Aakriti Pandita; Marisha Burden
bibliographic.citation_apa: Maw, A. M., Pandita, A., & Burden, M. (2026). Hospitalists are already using AI—why implementation will determine its impact. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 28, e97419. https://doi.org/10.2196/97419

methodology.technology_context: LLM-based platforms used by hospitalists for clinical decision support, including differential diagnosis and management options

eligibility.decision_rationale: Peer-reviewed commentary on LLM adoption and governance lag in hospital medicine; relevant as contextual evidence on organizational governance and implementation in a regulated domain, but it does not study conversational systems or conversational governance mechanisms.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Extracted metadata conflated correspondence address with title; article is a commentary linked to a related study and requires human confirmation of role as contextual rather than central evidence.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate as opinion/commentary synthesizing cited literature and implementation-science arguments; not an empirical study, so sampling and data-collection criteria are largely not applicable.

cerqual.explanation: The argument is coherent and clearly framed, but as a short commentary without primary data or direct analysis of conversational governance, its adequacy and confidence for answering governance-of-conversational-LLM questions are limited.

coding.theme: Implementation quality and organizational readiness as determinants of LLM impact in clinical practice
coding.subtheme: Governance and training lag behind clinician-led LLM use

synthesis.main_claim: High rates of hospitalist LLM use will not by themselves improve care; impact depends on implementation quality, training, workflow design, and ongoing evaluation.
synthesis.contribution: Frames LLM adoption in hospital medicine as an implementation-science problem and argues that organizational guidance, training, and monitoring must catch up with clinician use.
synthesis.limitations: Commentary format without original empirical methods; limited direct treatment of conversational interfaces, auditability, guardrails, or formal governance mechanisms.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence on governance lag, clinician-led LLM use, and implementation priorities in regulated healthcare; not suitable as central evidence on conversational governance architectures or controls.

evidence.claim: Article is a JMIR commentary on AI adoption in hospital medicine.
evidence.excerpt: Commentary Hospitalists Are Already Using AI—Why Implementation Will Determine Its Impact

evidence.claim: LLM-based platforms are widely used by hospitalists without adequate system guidance.
evidence.excerpt: two-thirds of hospitalists are using AI, particularly large language model (LLM)–based platforms, in their clinical work

evidence.claim: Organizational guidance, training, and governance are lagging adoption.
evidence.excerpt: outpacing the development of organizational guidance, training, and governance

evidence.claim: Clinicians adopt LLM tools faster than health systems can guide and govern them.
evidence.excerpt: clinicians adopting AI tools faster than health systems can guide and govern their use

evidence.claim: Use occurs largely outside health system integration and structured risk guidance.
evidence.excerpt: most commonly large language model (LLM)–based tools, and were doing so largely in the absence of health system integration

evidence.claim: Primary use case is clinical decision support rather than conversational governance.
evidence.excerpt: using these tools primarily to support clinical decision-making, including generating differential diagnoses and management options

evidence.claim: Poor integration and training can make LLM-supported decision-making suboptimal.
evidence.excerpt: clinical-decision making supported by AI may be suboptimal when integration, training, and workflow design are inadequate

evidence.claim: Authors prioritize training, implementation frameworks, and ongoing evaluation.
evidence.excerpt: training clinicians on AI inputs and interpreting outputs, applying implementation science frameworks for AI deployment in clinical environments, and establishing strategies for ongoing evaluation

evidence.claim: Continuous monitoring and iterative adaptation are recommended.
evidence.excerpt: learning health system infrastructure can enable continuous monitoring and iterative adaptation

evidence.claim: LLM outputs vary by prompt and may be overly confident or erroneous.
evidence.excerpt: whose outputs vary by prompt input and can include overly confident, sometimes erroneous output that could negatively impact clinician decision-making
Keywords: artificial intelligence; generative AI; hospital medicine; clinical decision support systems; health care technology adoption

evidence.claim: No conversational AI or chatbot governance focus is present in the supplied text.
